This beetle is steering by the Milky Way.
While pushing a ball of poop.
In Africa, a dung beetle finds fresh dung, rolls it into a perfect ball, and has to get away. Fast.
Because other beetles will try to steal it.
The trick? Roll in a straight line. Any straight line. Away from the crowd.
First, it climbs on top of the ball and does a little dance.
It's taking a picture of the sky.
In daylight, that's easy. It uses the sun.
But some beetles roll at night. With no moon.
So how do they keep straight in the dark?
Scientists took them into a planetarium.
Stars off. They wandered in circles.
Then they showed just one thing. The Milky Way. A faint glowing stripe.
And to be sure, they gave the beetles tiny little hats.
Hats on, lost. Hats off, perfect lines.
A beetle, with a brain smaller than a grain of rice, using our galaxy as a map.
The first animal ever shown to do it.
All for a ball of poop.
